publisher: Ba, Kiros, Hinton · University of Toronto
title: Layer Normalization: average in a different direction, drop the batch, become a Transformer staple
summary: Batch normalization computes its mean and variance across training samples, so small batches break it and RNNs are awkward. Layer normalization computes them across all neurons in one layer for a single sample, making it independent of the batch. We work through the difference by hand, examine its invariances, RNN experiments, and weaknesses on convolutional networks, then look at how Transformer models have modified it twice.
ai_summary: In "Layer Normalization" (Ba, Kiros, Hinton; University of Toronto, 2016), the authors switch batch normalization's "statistics across a batch of samples" to "mean and variance across all neurons in the same layer for a single sample," then re-scale by a learned gain and add a bias. It does not depend on batch size, computes identically at training and test time, and can be applied separately at every RNN time step. The paper analyzes its invariance to scaling and shifting the whole weight matrix and to scaling individual samples, and shows faster training on tasks including image-text retrieval, reading comprehension, sentence representation, DRAW, and handwriting generation; on convolutional networks it is weaker than batch normalization.
brief: Problem: Batch normalization depends on batch size, behaves differently at training and test time, and is awkward for RNNs with variable-length sequences.
Method: For each sample, compute the mean and variance across all neurons in the same layer, normalize, then apply a learned gain and bias.
Result: It is independent of batch size and can be computed at every time step. RNN-style tasks generally train faster, with better results on image-text retrieval, sentence representation, and more.
Limits: It underperforms batch normalization on convolutional networks. Later, in Transformers, it moved to the sublayer input and was simplified to RMSNorm.

cover.headline: Layer Normalization: a close reading of the original paper
cover.highlight: Normalize per sample, not per batch

nodes.label: Subtract mean, divide by standard deviation

sections.h: The bottom line: what the paper actually did

blocks.p: In July 2016, Jimmy Lei Ba, Jamie Ryan Kiros, and Geoffrey Hinton at the University of Toronto released this paper. The first author was also one of the authors of the earlier close reading of "Adam."

It aims to improve on batch normalization, introduced by Google a year earlier. Batch normalization works like this: for every neuron in the network, look at its inputs over the current batch of training examples, compute their mean and variance, and standardize the inputs to mean 0 and variance 1. It made feed-forward networks train much faster, but it has two hard limitations: its effect depends on batch size, so tiny batches fail; and it is hard to apply to recurrent neural networks (RNNs), because each time step would need its own statistics.

Layer normalization changes only one thing: instead of computing statistics across samples in a batch, it computes them across all neurons in the same layer for the same sample. Each sample is normalized on its own, regardless of what else is in the batch or how large it is. Training and test time use exactly the same computation, and applying it to an RNN means computing the statistics once at each time step.

The paper evaluates six task families, with emphasis on RNNs: image-text retrieval, reading comprehension, sentence representation, image generation, handwriting generation, and MNIST classification. Layer normalization generally trains faster and often produces better results. On convolutional networks, however, it does not beat batch normalization.

At the time the paper was aimed mainly at RNNs, but what eventually made it a building block was the Transformer. From the original 2017 Transformer through GPT-2 and LLaMA, nearly every layer relies on layer normalization or a simplified version of it.

callout.title: In one sentence
callout.text: Batch normalization: for the same neuron, compute mean and variance across a batch of examples. Layer normalization: for the same example, compute mean and variance across all neurons in a layer. Change the direction, and the dependence on the batch disappears.

callout.title: Three small concepts you'll need
callout.text: If you don't know them, these three are enough:
list: **Neuron input (summed input)**: the previous layer's output is multiplied by weights and summed, written a. This is what gets normalized, before the bias is added and before the activation function.
**Standardization**: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation so a set of numbers has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
**Recurrent neural network (RNN)**: at each time step, the same weights process one word and pass the hidden state to the next step. See the "Seq2Seq" reading for more.

sections.h: Background: where batch normalization helps—and where it gets stuck

blocks.p: The paper starts with the problem: in a deep network, the gradient with respect to one layer's weights depends heavily on the previous layer's neuron outputs. If those outputs change in a highly correlated way, the next layer has to keep adapting. The batch normalization paper calls this "covariate shift" and proposes to standardize the inputs to every neuron:

parts.desc: the mean and standard deviation of this neuron's input over the whole training set
learnable gain, multiplied back to restore a suitable scale after normalization

formula.note: The expectation over the whole dataset is too expensive, so in practice we estimate it from the current mini-batch. The paper notes this places constraints on batch size and makes the method difficult to use in RNNs.

list: **Batch-size dependent**: with a small batch, the mean and variance estimates are poor; with batch size 1 they are impossible to compute. Online learning—or distributed training where the model is so large each device can hold only a very small batch—cannot use it.
**Training/test mismatch**: during training it uses the current batch's statistics; at test time it must use a running average accumulated during training.

**RNNs are awkward**: sentences vary in length, so a direct extension would store a separate set of statistics for every time step. If the test set contains a sentence longer than any training sentence, there is no stored statistic to use.

blocks.p: Batch normalization has a side benefit: because each batch differs, its statistics are noisy, which acts as a regularizer. Layer normalization gives that up.

sections.h: Layer normalization: averaging in the other direction

blocks.p: The paper's observation is that a layer's output changes often affect all neurons in the next layer together, in a correlated way, especially with activations such as ReLU whose outputs can change a lot. So it proposes to fix the mean and variance of the summed inputs inside each layer:

parts.desc: number of neurons in this layer
the mean and standard deviation over all neurons in this layer for the same sample. All neurons in the layer share this pair, but each sample has its own
per-neuron gain and bias, applied after normalization and before the activation, so the network can still express any scale and shift

formula.note: The only difference from batch normalization is the direction of averaging. The paper stresses that layer normalization places no constraint on batch size and can be used for pure online learning with batch size 1.

fig.title: Worked example: the same data give completely different results under the two normalizations
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: 4 neurons in a layer, 3 samples in a batch. The numbers are our own; Sample 3 is exactly 10 times Sample 1. Standard deviation is the population standard deviation.
fig.note: Under layer normalization, Sample 1 and Sample 3, which is 10 times larger, produce exactly the same result; the pattern of which neuron is larger within each sample is preserved. Under batch normalization, the result for Sample 1 depends on which batch it lands in: change the batch, and its output shifts from roughly −0.6 to 1.

callout.title: The two normalizations are like two ways of grading
callout.text: Batch normalization is like ranking by subject: for math, where do you stand in the class? Layer normalization is like looking at your own strengths: put all your grades side by side and see which subjects are relatively strong or weak. The first needs the whole class's scores; the second only needs your own transcript.

quiz.q: Why doesn't batch normalization work with batch size 1, while layer normalization does?
options: Layer normalization does not need to compute the standard deviation

Batch normalization computes variance across the samples in the batch, and a single sample has variance 0; layer normalization computes across all neurons in the same sample, independent of batch size
Layer normalization is only used at test time
quiz.why: Batch normalization computes statistics for each neuron across examples; with only one example, the variance is 0 and cannot be divided by. Layer normalization computes statistics for each example across neurons; as long as a layer has more than one neuron, it can be computed.

sections.h: In RNNs: compute once at each time step

blocks.p: At each step, an RNN's input is made from the previous hidden state and the current input: a_{t} = W_{hh} · h_{t−1} + W_{xh} · x_{t}. Layer normalization applies directly:

parts.desc: computed using only the inputs to this layer at the current time step, so sentence length doesn't matter
gain and bias, shared by all time steps

blocks.p: The paper explains why this suits RNNs: in a standard RNN, the average magnitude of the summed inputs to the recurrent units tends to grow or shrink at every step, which is the source of exploding and vanishing gradients. With layer normalization, uniformly scaling all inputs to a layer does not change the output, so the hidden-state dynamics become much more stable.

The supplementary material gives the exact LSTM recipe: apply layer normalization separately to "hidden state times weights" and "input times weights" before adding them, and do another normalization on the memory cell c_{t} before the tanh.

sections.h: Theory: what each normalization is insensitive to

blocks.p: The paper puts batch normalization, weight normalization (which divides by the length of the weight vector instead of the variance), and layer normalization into one framework: each subtracts μ, divides by σ, and then applies a gain and bias, with differences only in how μ and σ are computed. It then compares which transformations each is invariant to—transformations that leave the model's output completely unchanged.

fig.title: Invariance properties of the three normalization methods
fig.subtitle: From Table 1 of the paper. "Invariant" means the model output is unaffected by that transformation.
fig.note: The last row is unique to layer normalization: scaling a single sample does not change the prediction. That is the property behind Sample 1 and Sample 3 being identical in the worked example above.

blocks.p: **Why scaling a single sample does not affect layer normalization**: when sample x is scaled by δ, all inputs to this layer are scaled by δ, μ and σ are also scaled by δ, and (a − μ) / σ is unchanged. Batch normalization cannot do this, because its μ and σ also depend on the other samples in the batch.
The paper also analyzes learning through the geometry of parameter space (the Fisher information matrix), reaching two intuitive conclusions:

list: **Longer weights learn more slowly**: after normalization, if the whole weight vector becomes longer, the model's output stays the same, but σ also grows. A given update size then has less effect on the output. In effect, the weight length automatically lowers its own learning rate, providing an implicit early-stopping effect and making training more stable near convergence.

**The gain is easier to learn**: in a normalized model, the "size" of the weight is handled by the gain parameter alone. The paper derives that, when learning the gain, the effect of a parameter change on the output depends only on the size of the prediction error—not on the input scale as in ordinary models. It is therefore more robust to rescaling of inputs and parameters.

blocks.p: **One detail that differs from batch normalization.** The authors of recurrent batch normalization found the initial gain had to be chosen carefully, and set it to 0.1. The paper tries 1.0 and 0.1 for layer normalization and finds 1.0 clearly better, indicating layer normalization is not as sensitive to the initial scale as recurrent batch normalization.

**Convolutional networks are a weak spot.** The paper's preliminary experiments show layer normalization is faster than no normalization, but batch normalization is better. Its explanation: in fully connected layers, different neurons contribute roughly equally to the final prediction, so standardizing them together is fine. In convolutional networks, neurons whose receptive fields lie on the image edge are rarely activated, and their statistics differ greatly from the rest of the layer, so pooling them into a single mean is not appropriate. In the MNIST experiment, the paper also deliberately does not normalize the final softmax layer, because its output scale determines how confident the prediction is.

callout.title: "Layer normalization completely replaced batch normalization"
callout.text: Not really. On convolutional networks and image tasks, batch normalization remains common today, and the paper itself admits layer normalization is worse there. Layer normalization became the standard in sequence models—RNNs and later Transformers—where sentences vary in length, batches cannot be too large, and training and inference must be consistent. Those are exactly batch normalization's weak points.

list: **The supplementary material swaps the gain and bias.** In equation (15) of the supplementary material, α multiplies the normalized value (the gain) and β is added (the bias), but the text below calls α and β "additive and multiplicative parameters, respectively" and says α is initialized to 0 and β to 1. If the gain α really were initialized to 0, the layer's output would initially be all zeros. Given Section 6's statement that "gain is initialized to 1 and bias to 0," the supplementary text likely swapped the two.

**The "curvature becomes one-half" claim may have missed a square.** Section 5.2.2 says when the weight length doubles, σ also doubles, so the curvature along this direction becomes one-half of its original value. By the paper's own equation (13), the Fisher information block in this direction is proportional to 1 / σ^{2}, so after doubling it should be one-quarter. This does not change the conclusion that longer weights learn more slowly.

**The covariate-shift explanation was later challenged.** The paper follows the batch normalization paper in arguing that normalization works because it reduces covariate shift. A 2018 study by Santurkar et al. argues batch normalization mainly smooths the loss landscape, with little connection to covariate shift. Why normalization helps is still debated.

**Direct comparisons with batch normalization are limited.** The only head-to-head results are on MNIST classification and reading comprehension (where the batch normalization numbers come from another paper); for convolutional networks the paper gives only a description, no data.

sections.h: What came next: a Transformer staple, reworked twice

blocks.p: One year later, the Transformer placed layer normalization in every layer: each sublayer (attention or feed-forward network) is wrapped in a residual connection and then normalized, producing LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)) (see the Transformer close reading). From then on, it formed the backbone of the Transformer along with the residual connection. It later went through two major redesigns:

fig.title: How layer normalization moved around in major models
fig.subtitle: From the architecture sections of each paper.
rows: Moved to the input of each sublayer, plus one final layer at the end
At the input of each sublayer
fig.note: The GPT-2 paper says this arrangement resembles "pre-activation" residual networks. The LLaMA paper says placing normalization at the input improves training stability.

list: **Moved to the input (Pre-LN):** the original Transformer adds first, then normalizes. GPT-2 changed the order: normalize the sublayer input, compute the sublayer, then add back the residual. That leaves the residual path free of any normalization, so signal and gradients flow straight through and very deep models train more easily.

**Dropping the mean (RMSNorm):** in 2019, Zhang and Sennrich proposed dividing only by the root mean square, without subtracting the mean; performance is similar but computation is cheaper. LLaMA adopted it, and many open-source large models have followed since.

blocks.p: The next article on this route shifts focus: the model sees tokens, not characters. **BPE subword tokenization** decides what a token is.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you get it?

quiz.q: If you multiply all the inputs of a single training example by 10, what happens to a layer-normalized network's prediction for that example?
options: The prediction is also multiplied by 10.
Unchanged: the layer's inputs, μ, and σ are all multiplied by 10, so the standardized values are the same.
It depends on the other examples in the batch.
quiz.why: This is layer normalization's unique "single training case re-scaling" invariance (the last row in Table 1 of the paper). Batch normalization cannot match it, because its statistics also depend on the other examples in the batch.

quiz.q: Why is layer normalization worse than batch normalization on convolutional networks?
options: In convolutional layers, neurons at different positions have very different statistical properties, for example those near image edges are rarely activated, so computing one mean and variance across all of them is a poor fit.
quiz.why: Layer normalization assumes the neurons in a layer are roughly comparable and can be standardized together. Fully connected layers mostly satisfy this; convolutional layers do not. The paper says this needs further study.

quiz.q: What two changes did layer normalization undergo between the original Transformer and LLaMA?
options: It switched back from layer normalization to batch normalization.
Its position moved from after the sublayer to before the sublayer input, and the normalization itself was simplified to RMSNorm, which divides only by the root mean square.
It is used only in the last layer.
quiz.why: GPT-2 moved it to the input of each sublayer, and LLaMA later switched to RMSNorm. Both changes make very deep models more stable to train and cheaper to compute.

blocks.p: After reading this piece, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: In which direction do batch normalization and layer normalization each compute the mean and variance?
What are the limitations of batch normalization, and how does layer normalization avoid them?
Why is layer normalization especially well-suited to RNNs?
What are the gain and bias for, and why are they applied after normalization?
Which transformations is layer normalization invariant to, and which is it not?
Why are longer weights said to automatically lower the learning rate?
How did the position of layer normalization in the Transformer change later?

None of those are in the paper this article follows.
